tags.gist: Supports the framework as a starting point but wants reversibility as its own explicit dimension, since anaphylaxis advice and allergen counseling differ in reversibility.
Wants clinicians to have a reliable way to verify what a device did or recommends and to reverse or override it, especially for higher-autonomy functions.
Asks CDRH to weight the setting's time pressure and make traceability to current practice parameters a core requirement as guidance evolves.
Agrees directiveness is judged by substance; wants manufacturers to document where each output type sits and test for unintended drift toward directiveness.
Says patient-facing tools deserve more weight than the framework implies, since patients misdescribe symptoms and a tool lacks a trained ear.
Notes many patients use tools instead of seeking care, so even low-risk-looking reassurance or remedies can cause harm.
Wants patient-facing advice devices to carry a persistent disclaimer, and a probably absent clinician backstop treated as a risk-elevating factor.
Says user training should inform risk; wants manufacturers to identify intended users' expected training and evaluate foreseeable generalist misapplication.
Supports trajectory evaluation; wants intended use defined by where a conversation plausibly ends, with multi-turn adversarial scripts probing drift.
Wants separate reporting by scenario severity with intentionally asymmetric criteria: very low tolerance for under-escalation near anaphylaxis, more for over-escalation.
Finds the framework reasonable but says training data must include real patient conversations, since patients describe symptoms inconsistently.
Wants experienced physicians practising in the relevant specialty involved during development, not only in later validation.
Wants guidance to state competency evaluation supplements postmarket accountability and to test handling of non-textbook presentations as its own evidence category.
Wants the framework to scale both benchmarking breadth and confirmation rigor, with patient-facing rescue-medication tools needing adjudication or prospective evaluation.
Calls the structure thorough and would add a clinical proficiency element for longitudinal chronic disease management reasoning.
Wants subgroup testing to explicitly require ethnically and racially diverse populations, plus pregnancy and pediatric age bands.
Would add a dedicated element on atypical, non-textbook and ambiguous presentations, where judgment matters most.
Wants construct validity shown by correlation with real outcomes, sponsor benchmarks independently validated with unseen items, results and rubrics shared with users.
Supports proportionality with a floor: severe-consequence action-directing devices cannot rely on retrospective review alone; favours shadow deployment with shared results.
Defers on methods but wants physicians in results review and evaluation distributions spanning multiple geographies and patient types.
Finds synthetic data fine for common presentations but risky for rare conditions; wants an independent non-GenAI reference dataset for any supplemented subgroup.
Would match the comparator to workflow: team performance where a physician reviews, device alone against a specialist panel for autonomous or patient-facing use.
Wants reviewers practising in the device's specialty represented on any panel judging specialist-level outputs.
Suggests a tiered panel, experts first then median clinicians, with practice guidelines anchoring the standard of care where relevant.
Sees no-device comparators as a useful supplement for access-expanding tools, but not a replacement for a specialist panel when available.
Supports societies holding specialty datasets and adjudicators, wanting third-party assessments published, conflicts disclosed and barriers to small developers avoided.
Finds the framework largely architecture agnostic; wants image-based devices tested across capture quality, lighting and skin tone.
Supports the trade only for lower-risk functions, not anaphylaxis or autonomous dosing, and wants near-real-time monitoring of safety-critical behaviors as a condition.
Finds the three approaches complementary; wants a minimum interval plus triggers such as model updates, and clinician review oversampling safety-critical interactions.
Wants two standing requirements: a prespecified severity-tiered response protocol for incorrect outputs and a fast, answered clinician feedback channel.
Worries a supervisor sharing the device's architecture shares its blind spots; wants ongoing physician review as the final layer for safety-critical flags.
Wants a required kill switch: a fast, human-controlled way to stop a device whose code is corrupted or output is harming patients.
Keeps primary monitoring responsibility with manufacturers, who hold the data; clinicians report and societies advise without taking on responsibility.
Says societies should not have to collect or review manufacturer data; participation should be voluntary and funded.
Wants manufacturers to maintain a transparent clinical review process, with authorization suspended if adequate monitoring and review prove impossible.
Says device-error liability should not fall solely on a physician nominally in the loop; asks CDRH to flag the gap to other authorities.
Says a one-time competency assessment cannot cover ongoing change from sponsor updates or uncontrolled foundation model changes.
Would scale re-evaluation to affected elements, fully re-benchmark safety after model or guardrail changes, and exclude open-ended model changes from PCCPs.
Suggests a tiered PCCP: narrow prespecified changes handled traditionally, broader evolution governed by a pre-authorized standing re-benchmarking protocol.
Would require contractual advance notice as a condition of authorization, safety re-benchmarking before deploying updates, user communication, and automated drift monitoring.
Supports master files and suggests an incentive: letting sponsors who reference one satisfy part of their benchmarking burden for model-level behaviors.
Wants devices offering clinical advice required to give health systems and physicians training, validation and subgroup results plus periodic real-world performance reports.
Wants tested human-confirmation checkpoints before irreversible actions, scaled to the risk framework, and attention to compounding error across long sequences.
Wants a required kill switch: a fast, human-controlled way to stop an agent mid-sequence before an irreversible action.
